section.title: Forgiveness for the Offender
section.sectionRationale: Church discipline had done its work: a man who had caused grief, likely by opposing Paul, had been punished by the majority and had repented. Now Paul turns the church from discipline to restoration. The punishment already imposed is enough; the danger now is not too little severity but too much. Paul urges them to forgive and comfort the offender, to reaffirm their love, lest excessive sorrow overwhelm him and lest Satan gain the advantage through an unforgiving church.
section.thesis: When a repentant offender has borne sufficient discipline, the church must move from punishment to forgiveness, comfort, and the reaffirming of love, forgiving as those who forgive in the presence of Christ, so that the sinner is restored and Satan gains no advantage over an unforgiving people.
section.frameNote: Two movements: the sufficient punishment of the offender and the call to forgive, comfort, and reaffirm love; and Paul's own forgiveness given in the presence of Christ, so that Satan should not outwit the church.

units.label: Sufficient punishment, now forgive
units.note: forgive and comfort, lest he be overwhelmed by sorrow

verses.text: Now if anyone has caused grief, he has not grieved me but all of you, to some degree, not to overstate it.
The punishment imposed on him by the majority is sufficient for him.
So instead, you ought to {{aphiemi|forgive}} and comfort him, so that he will not be overwhelmed by excessive sorrow.
Therefore I urge you to reaffirm your love for him.

units.label: Forgiven in the presence of Christ
units.note: so that Satan should not outwit us

verses.text: My purpose in writing you was to see if you would stand the test and be obedient in everything.
If you forgive anyone, I also forgive him. And if I have forgiven anything, I have forgiven it in the presence of Christ for your sake,
in order that Satan should not outwit us. For we are not unaware of his {{noema|schemes}}.

aphiemi.gloss: To send away, release, let go, forgive. The image is of releasing a debt or dismissing a charge, letting the offense go rather than holding it against the offender. It is the same verb Jesus uses when He teaches His disciples to pray for the forgiveness of debts. Here Paul urges the church to release the repentant man from the grip of his offense, joining forgiveness to comfort so that grace, not lingering condemnation, has the final word.

noema.gloss: A thought, design, scheme, or the mind that devises it. Paul uses the word for the calculated stratagems by which Satan seeks to harm the church. Here the devil's scheme is to turn discipline into destruction, to use an unforgiving spirit to crush a penitent believer and divide the body. Paul insists the church is not ignorant of such designs, so forgiveness becomes a weapon of spiritual warfare, guarding the flock from the enemy's cunning.

basic.context: A man in the church had caused serious grief, most likely by leading opposition against Paul. The church had disciplined him, and the discipline had worked: he had repented. Now Paul, far from demanding more severity, urges the opposite. The punishment already given is enough. It is time to forgive, comfort, and openly reaffirm love for him, so that he is not crushed by sorrow and so that Satan gains no foothold through an unforgiving church.
basic.hermeneutics: This is a case study in the goal of church discipline, which is always restoration, not destruction. Read verses 5 to 8 as the turn from punishment to forgiveness once repentance is real. Verse 11 reveals the spiritual stakes: unforgiveness is one of Satan's schemes. Paul models forgiveness done in the presence of Christ and for the sake of the whole body.
basic.originalLanguages: Paul urges the church to aphiemi, to forgive, to release the offender from his offense, the same verb Jesus uses for forgiving debts. And he warns that failing to do so plays into Satan's noema, his schemes or designs, the calculated stratagems the church must not be ignorant of.
basic.typology: The restoration of the repentant sinner reflects the God who does not deal with us according to our sins but removes our transgressions as far as the east is from the west. The church's forgiveness images the forgiveness of God in Christ, who welcomes back the penitent.
basic.christ: Paul forgives in the presence of Christ, so that Christ Himself is the pattern and the witness of the church's forgiveness. As Christ forgave freely and welcomes the repentant, so His people are to forgive and comfort. The whole ministry of reconciliation flows from the cross where forgiveness was purchased.
basic.god: God's heart is for the restoration of sinners, not their ruin. He disciplines, but His discipline aims at repentance and healing. The passage reflects a God who forgives the penitent and calls His people to mirror that mercy, guarding them against the enemy who would twist even good discipline into destruction.
basic.crossReferences: Matthew 18 gives Jesus' pattern for church discipline aimed at winning the brother. Galatians 6 calls the spiritual to restore the fallen gently. Ephesians 4 says forgive as God in Christ forgave you. Luke 15 shows the father running to welcome the returning son.
basic.oneStory: The Bible tells of a God who restores the repentant. Discipline is real, but its goal is always to bring the sinner back, and its end is forgiveness, comfort, and renewed love. In forgiving the penitent, the church displays the mercy of God in Christ and stands guard against the schemes of the enemy who wants an unforgiving people.

context.literary:
These seven verses are a parenthesis inside a travel story. Paul began explaining his changed plans at 1:15 and he will pick the account up again at 2:12, where he goes to Troas and cannot rest because Titus is not there. In between, 2:5 to 11 is a side step, yet it is hinged to what comes before. The vocabulary of grief runs straight through from 2:1 to 2:7: 'painful', 'grieve', 'saddened', 'distress', 'caused grief', 'sorrow'. The grief word group, lype and the verb lypeo, recurs again and again from 2:1 to 2:7. Paul had said that he wrote 'not to grieve you', 2:4, and now he turns to the one whose grief outran its usefulness.

The syntax of verse 5 is awkward in the Greek, and many commentators think Paul chose his words with care. He does not name the offender. He says 'if anyone has caused grief', speaking as though the matter were hypothetical, and he insists that the man has 'not grieved me but all of you'. Even the clause 'to some degree, not to overstate it' is a tactful hedge, literally 'in part, so that I do not burden you all'. The point is to move the focus from Paul to the community, and from blame to restoration.

The passage runs in three steps: a judgment on the discipline, verses 5 and 6, a command with three verbs, forgive, comfort, reaffirm, verses 7 and 8, and a reason in two layers, verses 9 to 11. The first reason is about obedience, 'to see if you would stand the test'. The second is spiritual strategy, 'in order that Satan should not outwit us'. The closing phrase, 'we are not unaware of his schemes', has a sober tone and sets the next section, where Paul speaks of triumph and of the fragrance of Christ, 2:14 to 16.

The conclusion of the matter appears later, in 7:5 to 16, where Titus brings news of the church's repentance and Paul rejoices.
context.historical:
The details of the case are partly hidden, and the church has asked for centuries who the offender was. Paul does not name him and the Corinthians knew who was meant. The best clues come from the surrounding chapters. Paul had made a painful visit, 2:1, in which someone seems to have publicly challenged or wronged him, and he followed it with a severe letter, 2:3 and 7:8. The church responded, and a 'majority' voted a punishment, 2:6. That detail tells us about how Corinth governed itself: the matter was settled by a community decision, not by an apostolic command from afar, and not unanimously. A minority had evidently not agreed. In the Jewish world discipline of this kind was known. The Dead Sea community of the same period decided matters of discipline in an assembly known as 'the many', and the Jerusalem church acted together in Acts 6:2 to 6 and 15:22.

The penalty is not described. The language of 'sufficient' and 'overwhelmed' suggests exclusion from fellowship or public censure, perhaps something close to the 'handing over' of 1 Corinthians 5:4 and 5. Any such sanction in a first century city mattered greatly. A person put out of a house church lost more than company. He lost the network that supplied meals, work and standing.

Corinth was a city of honor and shame. Public disgrace was heavy, and to be restored in public was as important as to be punished in public. Paul's request that the church 'reaffirm' love is a request for a visible act, in the open, with the community assembled. Verse 10 shows Paul himself joining the act: he forgives 'for your sake' and 'in the presence of Christ'.

The danger he names, that of Satan, belongs to Paul's reading of Corinth. He had warned of a Satan who disguised himself as an angel of light, 11:14, and the Corinthians' experience of the pagan city made them familiar with the idea of spiritual forces behind human behavior.
context.canonical:
The principle that discipline serves restoration is established across Scripture. The Lord says through the prophet that he takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked but in their turning, Ezekiel 18:23, and that 'the Lord disciplines the one He loves', Hebrews 12:6. In the New Testament the order of church discipline in Matthew 18:15 begins with the aim of winning the brother over, and it is followed at once by Peter's question about how often to forgive and Jesus' answer, 'not just seven times, but seventy-seven times', Matthew 18:21 and 22. Paul gives the same direction in Galatians 6:1: restore a person 'with a spirit of gentleness', and 2 Thessalonians 3:14 and 15, where the discipline aims to make a man ashamed but not to treat him as an enemy.

The relationship to 1 Corinthians 5 is important. There Paul had told the church to hand a sinning man over to Satan 'for the destruction of the flesh, so that his spirit may be saved', 1 Corinthians 5:5. The same writer now warns that Satan can also exploit an unforgiving church. Both discipline and its aftermath belong inside the same purpose of saving the person. Elsewhere Paul says that Hymenaeus and Alexander were handed over to Satan 'to be taught not to blaspheme', 1 Timothy 1:20, which fits the same corrective aim.

Forgiveness as Christ forgave is the next layer. The same Greek verb appears in Ephesians 4:32 and Colossians 2:13 and 3:13, tying the church's act to God's. Paul can also write in Ephesians 4:27 'do not give the devil a foothold', an echo of 2 Corinthians 2:11. The letter itself returns to the theme of godly sorrow in 7:9 to 11, to the ministry of reconciliation in 5:18 to 20, and to Satan's tactics in 11:3 and 14.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Paul writes to a church that has just won an argument and is in danger of losing the peace. The discipline he asked for succeeded, and the church had every reason to feel vindicated. His aim in these verses is to stop them from carrying the victory too far. He wants the discipline to end at the moment it has done its work. The sentence 'The punishment imposed on him by the majority is sufficient for him' sets a limit on discipline, which is something church leaders seldom do.

He also wants to protect the man. A person who has been shamed and cut off is at risk of being 'overwhelmed by excessive sorrow'. Paul is concerned for his soul and not only for his place in the church. At the same time he does not want the church to confuse the man's repentance with a loss of standards. He keeps the earlier discipline intact, calls it right, and builds the new step on it.

A third aim is to teach the church to think about spiritual strategy. Paul says Satan has designs, and one of them is to turn a good act into a destructive one. The enemy can attack a church by leading it to compromise sin, as in 1 Corinthians 5:1 and 2, and equally by leading it to harsh refusal of mercy. Paul wants the Corinthians to know that there are two ditches and that both belong to the adversary.

Finally, Paul wants the Corinthians to see that his own authority and theirs are joined. He forgives 'for your sake' and expects them to act as a body.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The details of the offense, the exact penalty and the identity of the man are described rather than prescribed. We cannot read from them a manual of procedure, with a number of votes or a length of exclusion. What the passage prescribes is the logic that governs such cases. Discipline has a purpose, and when the purpose is met, the discipline ends. Forgiveness is not something that happens only inwardly. It is shown in words and action, including comforting the person and 'reaffirming' love openly. And leaders should think about the effect of their decisions on the person being disciplined.

The passage does not say that every sin is to be forgiven with no consequences. The church's earlier action stands. It does not say that repentance can be skipped, either, since the case turns on the offender's response. Nor does it ask a victim to put themselves at risk. Paul himself was one of the people wronged, and he says that he forgives. A reader should take care when applying the passage to cases of abuse or ongoing harm, where wisdom about safety and accountability remains necessary. The passage describes a repentant person who has borne a sufficient penalty, and it is for that case that it commands.

debates.question: Is the offender the man of 1 Corinthians 5 or someone else?

views.label: The man who lived with his father's wife
views.case: Many early interpreters identified the two cases. Paul told the church to discipline that man, 1 Corinthians 5:1 to 5, and here he asks the church to restore someone who had repented. The key word 'handed over' and the language of destruction link them.

views.label: A man who opposed Paul at the painful visit
views.case: The grief here is said to have been caused to Paul and the whole church, and it follows the painful visit, 2:1, and the tearful letter, 2:3 and 4. Paul says that his purpose in writing was to test their obedience, 2:9, which suits a challenge to his authority better than a case of immorality. And 7:12 distinguishes 'the one who did wrong' from 'the one who was harmed', which suggests a personal wrong with a victim, perhaps Paul or one of his helpers.

debates.bearing: The passage does not require us to decide. In both cases the man had repented, a discipline had been applied, and the next duty was the same: forgive, comfort and reaffirm love.

debates.question: What does 'in the presence of Christ' mean in 2:10?

views.label: Before the face of Christ, as witness and judge
views.case: The Greek says 'in the face of Christ' (en prosopo Christou). Paul uses the word face again in 4:6 for the glory of God 'in the face of Jesus Christ'. On this reading, Paul acts with the Lord looking on, and his forgiveness must be what Christ would approve.

views.label: In the person or on behalf of Christ
views.case: Others take the phrase to mean 'as Christ's representative', since a person's face could stand for the person himself. Paul forgives as an apostle acting with Christ's authority and in his name.

debates.bearing: Both readings tie Paul's forgiveness to Christ, whether as a witness or an authority. They agree that forgiveness among Christians is never merely a private matter between two people. It is carried out under the eye of the Lord and for the sake of his church.

study.originalLanguages:
The vocabulary of these verses is more precise than the translations can show. The first thing to notice is a correction to a common assumption. The verb behind 'forgive' in verses 7 and 10 is not the one most often used for forgiveness in the Gospels. It is charizomai, from charis, grace. It means to give freely, to grant as a favor, and it is the same verb used for forgiving in Ephesians 4:32, Colossians 2:13 and 3:13, and Luke 7:42, where the moneylender 'forgave' both debtors. To forgive, in Paul's vocabulary here, is to treat a person with grace. Paul uses the verb four times in verses 7 and 10, including of himself, so it is a continuing theme.

Second, 'sufficient', hikanos, in verse 6. It means enough, adequate, and it can describe a quantity or a quality. Paul has used the word of his own fitness for ministry in 2:16 and 3:5. Applied to punishment it is a measure and a limit: the penalty is enough for its purpose. The word 'punishment' itself, epitimia, is a legal term for a penalty and is unusual in the New Testament. 'By the majority' is literally 'by the more', hypo ton pleionon, which tells us that not every member agreed.

Third, 'overwhelmed' in verse 7. The Greek verb is katapino, to swallow down. It is used of the sea swallowing the Egyptians in Hebrews 11:29 and of death 'swallowed up in victory' in 1 Corinthians 15:54. Paul has an image of a man swallowed whole by his own grief, drowned in sorrow. The same verb appears in 1 Peter 5:8, where the devil prowls 'seeking someone to devour'. The echo is probably deliberate: excessive sorrow can do the adversary's work.

Fourth, 'reaffirm', kyroo, in verse 8. This is a legal verb meaning to ratify or confirm formally. It is the verb used in Galatians 3:15 for a covenant that is 'ratified'. So Paul is not asking for private warmth but for a public act of confirmation, a formal restoring of the man to the community, as a covenant is confirmed.

Fifth, 'outwit' in verse 11. The verb is pleonekteo, from a root that means to have more, to take advantage. Paul says in 7:2 that he has taken advantage of no one, using the same family of words. The picture is of an opponent who gains an edge by fraud or by a move no one saw coming. The word for 'schemes' is noemata, thoughts or designs. In this letter Paul uses it of minds that have been hardened, 3:14, blinded, 4:4, led astray, 11:3, and of thoughts that he takes captive, 10:5. Satan's tactics are aimed at the mind, and the church's defense is clear thinking.

typology.fulfillment: Joseph's brothers feared that after Jacob's death he would repay them, and he wept and answered with comfort, 'Joseph reassured his brothers and spoke kindly to them', Genesis 50:15 to 21. The pattern is the same as Paul's three commands: forgive, comfort, reaffirm. The escalation is that the one who forgives in Christ does so out of a greater forgiveness, Ephesians 4:32. The type has limits, because Joseph spoke as one who had been raised to power over his brothers, while the church speaks as a body of forgiven sinners, none of them above the offender.

typology.type: The Day of Atonement and the sin carried away
typology.fulfillment: On the Day of Atonement the priest confessed Israel's sins over the live goat, and it carried them away into the wilderness, Leviticus 16:21 and 22. The people saw their guilt removed, as far as the east is from the west, Psalm 103:12. In Christ the removal is complete: God was 'not counting men's trespasses against them', 2 Corinthians 5:19. The church's forgiveness of a repentant man points to that removal. The pattern fails if it is taken as a replacement, for the church does not bear sin away. It only reflects the forgiveness that Christ has already won.

Peter denied his Lord three times, and the risen Christ asked him three times, 'Do you love Me?' and gave him sheep to feed, John 21:15 to 17. A failed disciple was not left in shame but returned to service. The restored man in Corinth is in a like position: disciplined, repentant and to be brought back. The escalation is that Peter was restored by Christ himself, with his own voice. The church acts as Christ's body in the same task. The pattern is limited in that Peter's restoration included a renewed commission, and Paul does not say the Corinthian man was given a role.

In the parable, the father sees his son 'while he was still in the distance' and runs to embrace him, Luke 15:20. The father does not wait for a full account of the past before showing love. Paul asks the Corinthians to behave as that father does: to reaffirm love after repentance. The story points to the heart of God, and Paul's instruction makes it the pattern for the community. The picture falls short if used as a rule for all cases, since the parable does not discuss sanctions or the care of those harmed, and it needs the rest of the New Testament to fill in the pattern.

study.christ:
The passage leads to Christ most directly through the word forgive. The verb Paul uses here, charizomai, is the verb for what God did in Christ. 'He forgave us all our trespasses, having canceled the debt ascribed to us in the decrees that stood against us. He took it away, nailing it to the cross!' Colossians 2:13 and 14. Ephesians 4:32 says 'forgiving each other just as in Christ God forgave you', and Colossians 3:13 says 'Forgive as the Lord forgave you'. Paul's request to the Corinthians is therefore not a new moral demand. It brings the church's life into line with the cross. A church that cannot forgive a repentant man is in the position of the servant in Matthew 18:23 to 35, who had been forgiven a huge debt and refused to forgive a small one.

Next, the phrase 'in the presence of Christ' puts the whole matter before the face of the Lord. In 4:6 Paul speaks of the 'face of Jesus Christ' as the place where the glory of God is known. When he says he forgives 'in the face of Christ', he is saying that a forgiving act is something done before the one who has himself forgiven. He is also reminding the church that Christ is the judge before whom discipline will be reviewed, 5:10.

Christ also appears as the model of the restoration. He prayed on the cross, 'Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing', Luke 23:34. He restored Peter after his denial, John 21:15 to 17. He is the shepherd who seeks the lost sheep, Luke 15:4 to 7. And the work of reconciliation to which Paul refers in 5:18 to 20 is the work in which Christ was 'not counting men's trespasses against them'. The ministry of the church toward a repentant offender is a small instance of that ministry.

There is also a contrast. Judas felt remorse and 'went away and hanged himself', Matthew 27:3 to 5, while Peter wept and was restored. One kind of sorrow ends in death and the other in life, as 7:10 says: 'Godly sorrow brings repentance that leads to salvation without regret, but worldly sorrow brings death.' Paul wanted the Corinthian man to know the first, and the church's welcome was the way Christ's welcome would reach him.

A caution is needed. The passage does not say that church forgiveness replaces Christ's forgiveness, or that a church can absolve sin on its own authority. It also does not turn the offender into a figure for Christ or for Judas. The links above come from the New Testament's own use of the language of forgiveness, and what the passage adds is a picture of Christ's forgiveness acted out in an ordinary congregation.
study.god:
The God of this passage is a God who limits his own discipline. The text does not say it directly, but the logic is the logic of Scripture: 'He has not dealt with us according to our sins or repaid us according to our iniquities', as Psalm 103:10 puts it. When Paul says 'sufficient', he is reasoning from the character of God, who disciplines for a purpose and then restores. Hebrews 12:10 and 11 says that God disciplines us 'for our good, so that we may share in His holiness', and that it 'yields a harvest of righteousness and peace'. Discipline in God's hands is a means, never an end.

He is also the God who keeps a church from two kinds of failure. Paul does not tell the Corinthians to forget the offense. He expects them to have taken it seriously and to have acted. God's holiness is not set aside. But the same God is rich in mercy, and the church must reflect that. This is a God who holds truth and grace together, John 1:14, without letting one swallow the other.

The passage also presents God as one who is concerned with the inner life. 'Excessive sorrow' is not just a social problem; it threatens to swallow a person. God's care extends to a man's emotional and spiritual condition. This is consistent with the God who 'heals the brokenhearted and binds up their wounds', Psalm 147:3, who does not break a bruised reed, Isaiah 42:3.

Another truth is the reality of spiritual opposition. God is sovereign, and still Paul can say that Satan has schemes. The adversary is real, but limited: he can outwit a church only if the church is unaware. God has given his people knowledge and the Spirit's wisdom to see these schemes, and they are not to be passive.

And God is the one in whose presence everything is done. Paul does not forgive in secret. The fact that a Christian forgives in front of Christ means that the whole life of the church is lived before him.

For worship, the passage teaches that a people who sing of mercy must practice mercy. The congregation's treatment of its repentant members is a kind of liturgy, an enacted hymn about the God who forgives. And a congregation that recognizes the adversary's schemes will pray for the restored as well as the wounded, for both are in danger.

crossReferences.note: Jesus gives the pattern for confronting a brother who sins, aimed at winning him back, and then tells Peter to forgive seventy-seven times. The passage shows that the call to forgive in 2 Corinthians 2:7 follows the Lord's own order: confront, call to repentance, then forgive without keeping count.

The spiritual are told to restore a person caught in a trespass 'with a spirit of gentleness' and to watch themselves. It supplies the attitude of 2 Corinthians 2:7 and 8, and reminds the community that the one restoring can be tempted too.

Believers are told not to let anger linger or to give the devil a foothold. It describes the same opening that Paul has in mind in 2 Corinthians 2:11, where a refusal to forgive gives the enemy an advantage.

Believers are to be kind and forgiving to each other just as in Christ God forgave them. The verb for forgive is the same as in 2 Corinthians 2:7 and 10, and the verse supplies the standard: the forgiveness of God in Christ.

Paul tells believers to bear with one another and to forgive 'as the Lord forgave you'. It is a general rule that matches the specific case of the Corinthian offender and grounds church life in the Lord's example.

Paul commands the church to remove a man who was sinning grossly so that his spirit might be saved. If it is the same man, 2 Corinthians 2 is the sequel. If it is not, the two cases still show the same two sides of the same purpose: serious sin dealt with, and a repentant sinner restored.

Paul tells how the sorrowful letter produced godly sorrow, repentance, earnestness and zeal in the church. It is the report of the outcome that 2:5 to 11 anticipates, and the key to the term 'excessive sorrow': the sorrow that Paul wanted was the kind that leads to repentance, not despair.

Those who disobey are to be set apart so that they might be ashamed, yet not treated as enemies but warned as brothers. The verse balances firmness and care, and shows that the same apostle ordered both discipline and kindness.

The father sees his returning son from a distance, runs to him and restores him with a robe, ring and feast. It is the clearest picture in the Gospels of the welcome Paul asks the church to give. It also shows the danger of the elder brother, who refused to join the celebration.

Jesus restores Peter after his denial by three questions and a renewed charge. It shows how restoration is more than the absence of punishment: it is a return to belonging and to trust, which is what 'reaffirm your love' means.

Peter warns that the devil prowls around seeking someone to devour, and tells believers to resist him, firm in the faith. The verb 'devour' is the same word as 'overwhelmed' in 2 Corinthians 2:7, so Peter and Paul seem to agree that the adversary attacks through sorrow and isolation.

Whoever brings back a wanderer from the truth will save his soul from death and cover over a multitude of sins. It shows that restoration is a work of salvation, and that the church's patience with a repentant sinner is a serious ministry and not just good manners.

study.oneStory:
The story of the Bible is a story of broken relationships and of the God who restores them. In Genesis 3 the first sin breaks fellowship, and the first words of God to the guilty are a search, 'Where are you?' The cost of sin is exile, but the promise of a rescuer begins in the same chapter. Throughout the Old Testament the pattern is repeated: the people sin, discipline falls, and God calls them back. Hosea's marriage and the prophets' promises of a return from exile say that God's discipline is never the last word.

The Old Testament also gives the church a pattern for community discipline. The sin of one affects the camp, Joshua 7, and the camp must deal with it. But the law is full of provisions for atonement and restoration, and the Day of Atonement is a yearly picture of guilt carried away. Joseph's forgiveness of his brothers shows what it looks like when a wronged person chooses grace.

Christ brings these threads together. He does not merely teach that sinners should be forgiven; he pays for the forgiveness at the cross. 'God was reconciling the world to Himself in Christ, not counting men's trespasses against them', 2 Corinthians 5:19. When the risen Lord restores Peter, he shows what kind of church he is building, one in which failure is not final. And he gives his church the ministry of reconciliation and the authority to bind and loose, Matthew 18:18, which is to be used for restoration.

The church is thus a community of the forgiven who must forgive. Its discipline is serious, because sin is serious, and its mercy is wide, because the cross is wide. Paul's advice to Corinth shows how a congregation can fall into either error, and his reference to Satan shows that the whole matter belongs to the larger conflict that began in the garden, where the serpent worked on a mind with a lie. Paul does not want the church to be 'led astray', 11:3, or outwitted.

The end of the story is a people without sin and without sorrow. In the new creation there will be no more death or mourning or crying or pain, Revelation 21:4. The offended and the offender will stand together before the one who forgave them both, and every debt will be settled. Until then, every act of forgiveness in a church, quiet and costly, is a down payment on that day.

quiz.q: What does Paul urge the church to do with the repentant offender?

options.text: Forgive him, comfort him, and reaffirm their love for him.
options.note: Verses 7 and 8 name all three: forgive, comfort, and reaffirm love.

options.text: Forgive him but keep him at arm's length.
options.note: Paul calls for active comfort and reaffirmed love, not distant tolerance.

options.text: Impose a stricter punishment to be sure he has learned.
options.note: Paul says the punishment already given is sufficient; more would be excessive.

options.text: Expel him permanently from the church.
options.note: The goal is restoration, not permanent exclusion.

quiz.q: Why does Paul say the punishment already given is sufficient?

options.text: Because the man has repented, and further sorrow could overwhelm him.
options.note: Verse 7 warns against his being overwhelmed by excessive sorrow.

options.text: Because discipline never accomplishes anything useful.
options.note: Discipline had done its work; Paul values it, but its aim is now met.

options.text: Because the offense was not really serious.
options.note: The grief was real; the point is that repentance has come, not that sin was trivial.

options.text: Because Paul no longer cared about the matter.
options.note: Paul cares deeply, which is why he seeks the man's restoration.

quiz.q: In whose presence does Paul say he forgives?

options.text: In the presence of Christ, for the sake of the church.
options.note: Verse 10 grounds forgiveness before Christ and for the body's good.

options.text: In the presence of the church elders only.
options.note: The elders may witness it, but Paul names Christ Himself as the witness.

options.text: In private, where no one could see.
options.note: Paul's forgiveness is open and for the church's sake, not hidden.

options.text: In the presence of the offender alone.
options.note: Paul forgives before Christ and for the sake of all, not merely privately to the man.

quiz.q: Why is forgiving the offender described as spiritual warfare?

options.text: So that Satan should not outwit the church, whose schemes they know.
options.note: Verse 11 frames forgiveness as guarding against Satan's designs.

options.text: Because forgiveness earns a reward in the battle against evil.
options.note: Forgiveness protects the church; it is not a merit that earns reward.

options.text: Because Satan cannot tempt a forgiving person at all.
options.note: Forgiveness closes one door to the enemy, but believers still face temptation.

options.text: Because unforgiveness has no spiritual consequences.
options.note: Paul says the opposite: unforgiveness gives Satan an advantage.

questions: The goal of discipline is restoration, not destruction. Is there someone you have disciplined or corrected whom God may now be calling you to forgive, comfort, and welcome back?
Paul warns against a penitent being overwhelmed by excessive sorrow. Do you tend to withhold comfort from those who have repented, and how might you actively reaffirm your love for them?
Paul forgave in the presence of Christ. How does remembering that Christ witnesses and grounds your forgiveness change the way you forgive those who have wronged you?
Unforgiveness is named as one of Satan's schemes. Where might a refusal to forgive be giving the enemy an advantage in your life or your church?
Reaffirming love means making forgiveness visible, not merely internal. What concrete step could you take this week to restore a relationship damaged by sin?

translationNotes.note: With to some degree, not to overstate it, Paul softens the statement so as not to exaggerate the injury.
Forgive renders aphiemi, to release or let go, the same verb used for forgiving debts; it pictures releasing the offender from the hold of his offense.
Schemes renders noema, meaning thoughts, designs, or stratagems; Paul warns that the church is not ignorant of Satan's calculated designs against it.
